summary.text: The proof rewrites the partial sums (for nonnegative parameters) as \([x^N]Q(x)(1+x)^{(m+2)N}\), where \(Q(x)=(1-x^2)/(1+x+x^2)\) has coefficients unchanged when their indices are multiplied by \(p\), and expands \((1+x)^p=1+x^p+pE_p(x)\) with \(1+x+x^2\mid E_p(x)\). The resulting correction polynomials are anti-palindromic, so pairing complementary coefficients reduces divisibility to a binomial-determinant factorization and factorial valuation bounds, yielding three new powers of \(p\) at each scaling; negative parameters are reduced to the nonnegative case by a sign-reversing involution plus a boundary binomial term with the same scaling congruence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}=1+x+2x^2+5x^3+\cdots .
\]
It is characterized as the unique formal power series with constant term 1 satisfying
\(c=1+xc^2\). For an integer \(r\) and an integer \(k\geq 0\), write
\[
 C_r(k)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&k=0,\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle \frac{r}{r+k}\binom{r+2k-1}{k},&k>0,
 \end{cases}
\]
where generalized binomial coefficients are defined by
\[
 \binom{z}{k}=\frac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-k+1)}{k!}\qquad(z\in\mathbb Z).
\]
When \(r+k\ne0\), the displayed quotient is an integer. It is the coefficient \([x^k]c(x)^r\), as follows from the usual Lagrange inversion formula applied to \(c=1+xc^2\). In the generalized sequence used below, if the displayed denominator is zero, the quotient is assigned the value zero. This convention only creates one exceptional endpoint in the argument, and it will be dealt with explicitly.

For \(m\in\mathbb Z\) and \(N>0\), define
\[
 a_m(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}C_{mN}(k),
 \qquad a_m(0)=1.
\]
For \(m=4\), no denominator vanishes, and this is precisely the sum of the coefficients through degree \(N\) of \(c(x)^{4N}\), hence the value at \(x=1\) of its degree-\(N\) Taylor truncation. Thus \(a_4(N)\) is OEIS A333096.

We prove the stronger assertion valid for every integral \(m\): if \(p\ge5\) is prime, \(N>0\), \(\ell\ge0\), and \(p^\ell\mid N\), then
\[
 a_m(pN)\equiv a_m(N)\pmod {p^{3(\ell+1)}}. \tag{1}
\]
Taking \(N=np^{k-1}\) and \(\ell=k-1\) will give the desired result.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Two elementary divisibility lemmas
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We begin with the source of the three extra powers of \(p\).

For natural numbers \(X,Y,d,e\), with \(d,e>0\), one has
\[
 d!e!\left(\binom Xd\binom Ye-\binom Xe\binom Yd\right)
   =XY(Y-X)z                                      \tag{2}
\]
for some integer \(z\).

Indeed, put
\[
 U_d(T)=\prod_{i=1}^{d-1}(T-i),\qquad
 U_e(T)=\prod_{i=1}^{e-1}(T-i).
\]
Since
\[
 d!\binom Td=T\,U_d(T),\qquad e!\binom Te=T\,U_e(T),
\]
the left side of (2) is
\[
 XY\bigl(U_d(X)U_e(Y)-U_e(X)U_d(Y)\bigr).
\]
Every polynomial takes congruent values at \(X\) and \(Y\) modulo \(Y-X\), so the expression in parentheses is divisible by \(Y-X\). This proves (2).

We shall also use the following factorial estimate. If \(p\ge5\), \(d,e>0\), and \(d\ne e\), then
\[
 v_p(d!)+v_p(e!)+3\le d+e.                       \tag{3}
\]
The standard estimate
\[
 (p-1)v_p(t!)<t\qquad(t>0)
\]
implies \(4v_p(t!)<t\), because \(p-1\ge4\). Applying this to \(d\) and \(e\), and using \(d\ne e\) to handle the integral rounding, gives (3). We shall also use the slightly coarser consequence
\[
 v_p((d+e)!)+3\le d+e                            \tag{4}
\]
when \(d,e>0\) and \(d\ne e\). Again this follows from \(4v_p((d+e)!)<d+e\), together with the fact that a sum of two distinct positive integers is at least 3.

For later coefficient manipulations define
\[
 \operatorname{Sub}(M,B,d)=
 \begin{cases}
 \binom M{B-d},&d\le B,\\
 0,&d>B.
 \end{cases}
\]
If \(A=B+Y\), \(j=d+e\le A\), then a direct factorial calculation gives
\[
 j!\binom Aj\operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,d)
 =\binom ABd!e!\binom Bd\binom Ye.               \tag{5}
\]
The formula remains valid when one of the binomial coefficients vanishes. Subtracting the formula with \(d,e\) interchanged yields
\[
 j!\binom Aj\bigl(\operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,d)
             -\operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,e)\bigr)
 =\binom ABd!e!\left(\binom Bd\binom Ye-
                         \binom Be\binom Yd\right). \tag{6}
\]

Suppose first that \(p^\ell\mid B\) and \(p^\ell\mid Y\). Then
\(p^{3\ell}\mid BY(Y-B)\). Equations (2) and (6) show that
\[
 p^{3\ell}\mid j!T,
 \quad
 T=\binom Aj\bigl(\operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,d)
             -\operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,e)\bigr).
\]
Using (4), we conclude that
\[
 p^{3(\ell+1)}\mid p^jT                         \tag{7}
\]
whenever \(d,e>0\), \(d\ne e\), and \(j=d+e\).

We will also need a version with an arbitrary initial exponent. If
\[
 p^L\mid BY(Y-B),
\]
the same argument gives \(p^L\mid j!T\), and (4) gives
\[
 p^{L+3}\mid p^jT.                              \tag{8}
\]

These are the divisibility statements used when terms indexed by \(d\) and \(j-d\) are paired.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The Frobenius error and its symmetry
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix a prime \(p\ge5\), and define the integral polynomial
\[
 E_p(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\frac1p\binom pi x^i.
\]
The divisibility of the interior binomial coefficients by \(p\) gives
\[
 (1+x)^p=1+x^p+pE_p(x).                          \tag{9}
\]

Let
\[
 \Phi(x)=1+x+x^2.
\]
We claim that \(\Phi\mid E_p\). First, modulo \(\Phi\), one has
\(x^3=1\) and \(1+x=-x^2\). A prime \(p\ge5\) is congruent to 1 or 2 modulo 3 and is odd. In either case, reducing powers modulo 3 shows
\[
 (1+x)^p\equiv1+x^p\pmod\Phi.
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) divides the left side of
\(pE_p=(1+x)^p-(1+x^p)\). Since \(\Phi\) is monic, division by it has integral remainder; if multiplying that remainder by the nonzero integer \(p\) gives zero, the remainder itself is zero. Hence \(\Phi\mid E_p\). Write
\[
 E_p(x)=\Phi(x)H_p(x).                           \tag{10}
\]
Since \(\deg E_p\le p-1\), we have \(\deg H_p\le p-3\).

The coefficients of \(E_p\) are symmetric because
\(\binom pi=\binom p{p-i}\). If reflection in degree \(D\) is defined by
\[
 f^*(x)=x^Df(x^{-1}),
\]
then, viewing missing endpoint coefficients as zero,
\[
 E_p^*=E_p\quad\text{in degree }p.
\]
Also \(\Phi^*=\Phi\) in degree 2. Reflecting (10) and cancelling the nonzero polynomial \(\Phi\) gives
\[
 H_p^*=H_p\quad\text{in degree }p-2.             \tag{11}
\]

Now define integers
\[
 q_0=1,
 \qquad
 q_n=\begin{cases}2,&n>0\text{ and }3\mid n,\\-1,&n>0\text{ and }3\nmid n,
 \end{cases}
\]
and let \(Q(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}q_nx^n\). A direct check in the three residue classes modulo 3 gives
\[
 (1+x+x^2)Q(x)=1-x^2.                            \tag{12}
\]
Moreover, because \(p\ne3\), multiplication by \(p\) preserves divisibility by 3, and hence
\[
 q_{pn}=q_n.                                     \tag{13}
\]

For \(j>0\), (10) and (12) give
\[
 Q(x)E_p(x)^j
 =(1-x^2)\Phi(x)^{j-1}H_p(x)^j=:K_{p,j}(x).      \tag{14}
\]
The right side is a polynomial. Reflection in degree 2 sends \(1-x^2\) to its negative; \(\Phi\) and \(H_p\) are reciprocal by (11). The framing degrees add to
\[
 2+2(j-1)+(p-2)j=pj.
\]
Consequently
\[
 x^{pj}K_{p,j}(x^{-1})=-K_{p,j}(x).              \tag{15}
\]
In coefficient form, if
\[
 c_d=[x^{pd}]K_{p,j}(x),
\]
then
\[
 c_{j-d}=-c_d\quad(0\le d\le j),                \tag{16}
\]
and \(c_0=0\). Coefficients with \(d>j\) vanish.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The main coefficient supercongruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For natural numbers \(A,B\), define
\[
 F(A,B)=[x^B]Q(x)(1+x)^A.
\]
We prove that if \(p^\ell\mid B\) and \(p^\ell\mid Y\), then
\[
 F(p(B+Y),pB)\equiv F(B+Y,B)
       \pmod {p^{3(\ell+1)}}.                    \tag{17}
\]

Put \(A=B+Y\). From (9) and the binomial theorem,
\[
 (1+x)^{pA}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{A}p^j\binom Aj E_p(x)^j
                    (1+x^p)^{A-j}.               \tag{18}
\]
The \(j=0\) term contributes
\[
 [x^{pB}]Q(x)(1+x^p)^A=F(A,B).                  \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, in the coefficient convolution, \((1+x^p)^A\) has nonzero coefficients only at exponents divisible by \(p\), and (13) changes \(q_{pt}\) to \(q_t\).

For \(j>0\), use (14). The corresponding correction term in (18), after multiplication by \(Q\) and extraction of \(x^{pB}\), is
\[
 \sum_{d=0}^{j}p^j c_d\binom Aj
       \operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,d).              \tag{20}
\]
Pair the term indexed by \(d\) with that indexed by \(e=j-d\). The endpoints vanish because \(c_0=c_j=0\). If \(d=e\), anti-symmetry gives \(c_d=-c_d\), hence \(c_d=0\). Otherwise \(d,e>0\) and \(d\ne e\), and the paired expression is
\[
 p^jc_d\binom Aj
 \bigl(\operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,d)
       -\operatorname{Sub}(A-j,B,e)\bigr),
\]
which is divisible by \(p^{3(\ell+1)}\) by (7). Thus every correction sum (20), and therefore their total, is divisible by that modulus. Equations (18) and (19) prove (17).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Identifying the Catalan partial sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

It is useful to remove the apparent denominator in \(C_r(k)\). For \(k>0\) and \(r+k\ne0\), the elementary adjacent-binomial identity gives
\[
 C_r(k)=
 \binom{r+2k-1}{k}-\binom{r+2k-1}{k-1}.          \tag{21}
\]
Let the right side, together with value 1 at \(k=0\), be denoted by \(D_r(k)\), and put
\[
 P(r,N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}D_r(k).
\]
We claim that for all natural \(A,N\),
\[
 P(A-2N,N)=F(A,N).                               \tag{22}
\]

Here is a formal-series derivation. Let \(B_z(x)=(1+x)^z\) be the generalized binomial series, and put
\[
 U=xB_{-2}(x),\qquad G_N=1+U+\cdots+U^N.
\]
Define
\[
 \mathcal B_{A,N}(x)=(1-x)B_{A-1}(x)G_N(x).
\]
Because \(B_uB_v=B_{u+v}\), and because
\[
 \Phi(x)B_{-2}(x)=1-U,
\]
a geometric-series calculation gives
\[
 \Phi(x)\mathcal B_{A,N}(x)
 =(1-x^2)B_A(x)(1-U^{N+1}).                      \tag{23}
\]
The factor \(U^{N+1}\) has order at least \(N+1\), so it does not affect coefficients through degree \(N\). By (12), the right side without this remainder equals
\(\Phi Q B_A\). Since \(\Phi\) has constant term 1, equality after multiplication by \(\Phi\) determines coefficients successively. Therefore
\[
 [x^N]\mathcal B_{A,N}(x)=[x^N]Q(x)(1+x)^A=F(A,N). \tag{24}
\]
On the other hand, expanding \(G_N\) and setting \(t=N-k\), the coefficient of degree \(N\) in the summand containing \(U^t\) is
\[
 [x^k](1-x)B_{A-1-2t}(x)
 =D_{A-2N}(k).
\]
Summing over \(k=0,\ldots,N\) proves (22).

If \(M\ge0\), put \(A=(M+2)N\). Then \(A-2N=MN\), and none of the relevant denominators in (21) vanishes (apart from \(k=0\), already separately defined). Hence
\[
 a_M(N)=F((M+2)N,N).                             \tag{25}
\]
Now assume \(p^\ell\mid N\). In (17), take
\[
 B=N,
 \qquad Y=(M+1)N.
\]
Both are divisible by \(p^\ell\), and (25) gives
\[
 a_M(pN)\equiv a_M(N)\pmod {p^{3(\ell+1)}}       \tag{26}
\]
for every \(M\ge0\).

There are two small exceptional negative values. For \(m=-1\), (21) is valid through \(k<N\), but at \(k=N\) its right side is \(-1\), whereas our zero-denominator convention gives \(C_{-N}(N)=0\). Thus
\[
 a_{-1}(N)=F(N,N)+1.                             \tag{27}
\]
Applying (17) with \(B=N,Y=0\) proves (1) for \(m=-1\); the added constant 1 cancels.

For \(m=-2\), no denominator vanishes for \(0<k\le N\), and (22) gives
\[
 a_{-2}(N)=F(0,N)=q_N.                           \tag{28}
\]
By (13), \(q_{pN}=q_N\), so (1) also holds for \(m=-2\), even as an equality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. An involution for the remaining negative parameters
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(S\ge2\), we establish
\[
 a_{-(S+1)}(N)=(-1)^N\left(
 a_{S-2}(N)+\binom{SN-1}{N-1}\right).            \tag{29}
\]

We give the coefficient argument. For \(R\ge2k\), the negative-binomial identity
\[
 \binom{-u}{k}=(-1)^k\binom{u+k-1}{k}
\]
applied to (21) gives
\[
 D_{-R}(k)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&k=0,\\
 (-1)^k\binom{R-k}{k}
 +(-1)^k\binom{R-k-1}{k-1},&k>0.
 \end{cases}                                    \tag{30}
\]
To sum these diagonal terms, put
\[
 V=-x(1+x),\qquad 1+V+\cdots+V^N=G_N^V,
\]
and
\[
 \mathcal N_{A,N}(x)=(1+2x)(1+x)^{A-1}G_N^V.
\]
Since \(\Phi=1-V\),
\[
 \Phi\mathcal N_{A,N}
 =(1+2x)(1+x)^{A-1}(1-V^{N+1}).                  \tag{31}
\]
The remainder again begins above degree \(N\). A direct use of (12) shows
\[
 \Phi\left(Q(x)(1+x)^A+x(1+x)^{A-1}\right)
 =(1+2x)(1+x)^{A-1}.                             \tag{32}
\]
Thus comparison through degree \(N\) in (31) and (32) yields
\[
 [x^N]\mathcal N_{A,N}
 =F(A,N)+\binom{A-1}{N-1}.                       \tag{33}
\]
Expanding instead in powers of \(V\), and using (30), gives
\[
 [x^N]\mathcal N_{A,N}
 =(-1)^N P(-(A+N),N).                            \tag{34}
\]
Taking \(A=SN\), and using (25) with \(M=S-2\), gives (29). For \(m=-(S+1)\), no zero denominator occurs for \(0\le k\le N\), so the formal and actual partial sums agree.

It remains to prove that the boundary term
\[
 H_S(N)=\binom{SN-1}{N-1}                        \tag{35}
\]
has the same scale supercongruence for every \(S\ge2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The boundary binomial coefficient
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We use a second coefficient series. Define
\[
 r_0=1,
 \qquad r_n=2(-1)^n\quad(n>0),
 \qquad R(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}r_nx^n.
\]
Then
\[
 (1+x)R(x)=1-x.                                  \tag{36}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
 r_{pn}=r_n.                                     \tag{37}
\]
Set
\[
 \mathcal R(A,B)=[x^B]R(x)(1+x)^A.
\]
We claim the strengthened scale result
\[
 p^L\mid BY(Y-B)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal R(p(B+Y),pB)\equiv\mathcal R(B+Y,B)
 \pmod {p^{L+3}}.                               \tag{38}
\]

The proof exactly parallels that of (17), so we record the needed changes. Since \(p\) is odd, substituting \(x=-1\) in (9) gives \(E_p(-1)=0\), and hence
\[
 E_p(x)=(1+x)J_p(x),
 \qquad \deg J_p\le p-2.                        \tag{39}
\]
The symmetry of \(E_p\), together with the reciprocity of \(1+x\), shows that \(J_p\) is reciprocal when framed in degree \(p-1\). From (36), for \(j>0\),
\[
 R(x)E_p(x)^j=(1-x)(1+x)^{j-1}J_p(x)^j=:L_{p,j}(x). \tag{40}
\]
Reflection in degree \(pj\) negates this polynomial, because \(1-x\) is anti-reciprocal and all other factors are reciprocal. Thus the coefficients
\([x^{pd}]L_{p,j}\) satisfy the same anti-symmetry under \(d\leftrightarrow j-d\), vanish at \(d=0,j\), and vanish for \(d>j\).

Expand \((1+x)^{pA}\) by (18), use (37) for the base term, and pair each correction term exactly as in (20). This time apply (8), whose hypothesis is precisely \(p^L\mid BY(Y-B)\). Every correction is divisible by \(p^{L+3}\), proving (38).

Formula (36) also evaluates \(\mathcal R\) explicitly:
\[
 \mathcal R(A,B)
 =[x^B](1-x)(1+x)^{A-1}
 =\binom{A-1}{B}-\binom{A-1}{B-1}.               \tag{41}
\]
For \(A=SN\), the adjacent-binomial relation gives
\[
 \mathcal R(SN,N)=(S-2)\binom{SN-1}{N-1}
 =(S-2)H_S(N).                                   \tag{42}
\]

First suppose \(S>2\), and put \(q=v_p(S-2)\). In (38), take
\[
 B=N,
 \qquad Y=(S-1)N,
 \qquad L=3\ell+q.
\]
Indeed,
\[
 BY(Y-B)=N\cdot(S-1)N\cdot(S-2)N

a is divisible by \(p^{3\ell+q}\). Therefore (38) and (42) give
\[
 (S-2)H_S(pN)\equiv(S-2)H_S(N)
       \pmod {p^{3\ell+q+3}}.
\]
Cancelling exactly the \(q\) powers of \(p\) in \(S-2\) gives
\[
 H_S(pN)\equiv H_S(N)\pmod {p^{3(\ell+1)}}.      \tag{43}
\]

The case \(S=2\) cannot be obtained by cancellation in (42), so we use a perturbation. We need the following continuity fact for binomial coefficients:
\[
 X\equiv Y\pmod {p^{E+v_p(k!)}}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \binom Xk\equiv\binom Yk\pmod {p^E}.            \tag{44}
\]
To prove it, compare the falling products
\(X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1)\) and
\(Y(Y-1)\cdots(Y-k+1)\). Every factor is congruent modulo the assumed power, so the products are congruent. They equal \(k!\binom Xk\) and \(k!\binom Yk\); removing the \(v_p(k!)\) powers contributed by \(k!\) proves (44).

Set
\[
 E=3(\ell+1),
 \quad v_0=v_p((N-1)!),
 \quad v_1=v_p((pN-1)!),
 \quad T=E+v_0+v_1,
 \quad S'=2+p^T.
\]
Then \(S'>2\), so (43) applies to \(S'\):
\[
 \binom{S'pN-1}{pN-1}
 \equiv
 \binom{S'N-1}{N-1}\pmod {p^E}.                 \tag{45}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 S'N-1\equiv2N-1\pmod {p^{E+v_0}},

a and
\[
 S'pN-1\equiv2pN-1\pmod {p^{E+v_1}}.
\]
By (44), the lower and upper binomial coefficients in (45) may therefore be replaced respectively by
\(\binom{2N-1}{N-1}\) and
\(\binom{2pN-1}{pN-1}\), modulo \(p^E\). Hence (43) holds also for \(S=2\). We have proved (43) for every \(S\ge2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Completion for every integer parameter
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now establish (1) by cases on \(m\).

* If \(m\ge0\), it is (26).

* If \(m=-1\), it follows from (27) and (17).

* If \(m=-2\), it follows from (28) and \(q_{pN}=q_N\).

* If \(m\le-3\), write \(m=-(S+1)\) with \(S\ge2\). Apply (29) at \(N\) and \(pN\). The nonnegative-parameter result (26), with parameter \(S-2\), gives
\[
 a_{S-2}(pN)\equiv a_{S-2}(N)
 \pmod {p^{3(\ell+1)}}.
\]
Equation (43) gives the same congruence for the boundary terms. Finally, because \(p\) is odd,
\[
 (-1)^{pN}=(-1)^N.
\]
Multiplying the sum of the two congruences by this common sign and using (29) proves (1).

Finally let \(n,k>0\), and put
\[
 N=np^{k-1},\qquad \ell=k-1.
\]
Then \(N>0\), \(p^\ell\mid N\), \(pN=np^k\), and
\(3(\ell+1)=3k\). Formula (1) therefore gives, for every \(m\in\mathbb Z\),
\[
 a_m(np^k)\equiv a_m(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}.
\]
Taking \(m=4\), for which \(a_4=a\) is exactly A333096, proves
\[
 \boxed{a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}}
\]
for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers \(n,k\), as required.
